Committee resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Chairman, at six o'clock we were discussing the desirability of placing the word * Canada ' after the name of the province in the proposed mark. I

wish to make myself clearly understood in my advocacy of the rights and interests of the people of Nova Scotia. Hon. gentlemen will remember that in the first instance, when this discussion arose, I asked to have the word ' Canadian ' struck out, so that the mark would read ' A No. 1 ' or ' No. 1.' That was objected to. I next asked, in ease that should not be agreed to, that the name of the province be put after ' No. 1 ' or 'A No. 1.' That is the question now under discussion. I believe the shippers of apples in Nova Scotia are so sensitive about the word ' Canada ' that if they were not free to use the name of the province, they would not avail themselves of section 6. But I do not wish to prolong the discussion, and I will not say a word more if a grade can be fixed, so that we can enforce a penalty under this Act, by providing something like this-I am not wedded to the particular words ; add the following to section 4 or insert it as a new section :
No person shall sell or offer, expose or have in his possession (or sale, any fruit packed in a closed package, on which package is marked anything which indicates that the (ruit contained in such package is of first or best or extra good quality, unless such fruit consists of well-grown specimens of one variety.
And so forth, the same as we have it now in sections 6 and 7. I am satisfied that if section 6 is left as it is desired to leave it by gentlemen from Ontario, our people in Nova Scotia will not avail themselves of it; but they are anxious to have a clause in the Act which will establish a grade. With this clause, they can call their fruit 1 A No. 1 ' or ' No. 1,' or ' A No. 1, Nova Scotia,' it they like. It is something which will allow them to have a distinctive grade for their fruit, and will not offend their sensitiveness with regard to the use of the word ' Canada.' I suppose we should feel flattered because gentlemen coming from the west are anxious to have that word tacked on to Nova Scotia, so that they can have the advantage of her fair reputation. The fruit-growers of Nova Scotia, while they feel flattered, are more concerned about their own interests.

I fancy that the hon. gentleman has flattered himself much more than Canada in the expressions to which he has given utterance. We in Ontario are fair enough to recognize what is good in Nova Scotia ; but I am sorry I cannot pay that compliment to the hon. gentleman for what he has just said. He took occasion this afternoon to speak of the honesty of the people of Nova Scotia. I have not a doubt that they are honest, but I have less doubt that they are any more honest than other people. I think they would be no less liable than other people to send bad fruit to market. I wish to point out to the Minister of Agriculture that it is important that
we should maintain as our first object in the English market the interests of Canada. Any departure from that would be a false step. Any apples packed for the British market should be known as coming from Canada, no matter whether they come from Nova Scotia, from Ontario, or from elsewhere. We in Ontario desire to be perfectly fair to the other provinces. If Nova Scotia is able to send a superior class of fruit to market, let it do so by all means; but let it be understood that the fruit comes from Canada. If the shippers of Nova Scotia have been able to earn a reputation there for their apples, surely they will be able to retain it. The suggestion of the hon. gentleman means a repetition in a sense of sections 6 and 7. If you fix a standard such as the hon. gentleman suggests, let that be a governing one for the whole Dominion. The question comes back to making it permissive for one province to step out and omit the word ' Canada.' If we are going to build up Canada, we must always understand that our fruit must be known as Canadian fruit. If each province desires to designate the fruit from that province, that is a proper thing to do. But anything short of that will not, I think, meet the views of this House.
No person feels aggrieved because in Manitoba they speak of No. 1 Manitoba hard wheat.
That is not a parallel case.
That is to say, a cereal is not a parallel case with fruit.
Because we do not grow such wheat anywhere else in Canada.

Therefore, I could understand that the people of Manitoba would feel very much aggrieved if their wheat were marked No. 1 Canadian, because then inferior wheat from Ontario, and still more inferior wheat from Nova Scotia, would be alowed to rank with it. If a particular province excels in a certain product, why should the fact not be indicated by the name of the province from which the product comes ? We cannot compete with Ontario in beef, and if all beef were marked as Canadian beef, it would be a great injustice to Ontario. So in a hundred other cases. Nova Scotia apples have made for themselves a reputation in Great Britain before Ontario or Quebec apples had any reputation there, and that reputation will continue ; and I think it would be a great injustice to Nova Scotia to enable the apples of the other provinces to rank with its apples. Take another case. In Prince Edward Island they produce the best potatoes grown in this Dominion. Owing to differences of soil and climate, certain articles grow better in one part of the country than they do in another, and it

would be very unfair to grade them all alike. As I understand, all that the hon. member for Annapolis is claiming is that as a reputation has been made for Nova Scotia apples, shippers should have the liberty of taking advantage of that fact.
Is Nova Scotia Canada ?

No.
Mr. FRASER, Nova Scotia was known before Canada was.
Does the hon. gentleman say that the word * Nova Scotia ' was known before the word 'Canada'?
No, but I can tell the hon. gentleman that long before the word ' Ontario ' was known, the word ' Nova Scotia ' was known.

I will not go into the history either of names or provinces, but I think my hon. friend from Annapolis has perhaps given a solution of this difficulty which will he satisfactory to him and still leave the Bill very much as it was originally. On Friday last, the hon. member for Bothwell pointed out that section No. 8 was vague, because there was no standard described as in sections 6 and 7. I see the force of his objection, and have drawn up an amendment to cover that point. I would suggest that the following be substituted for section 8 :
No person shall sell or offer, expose or have in his possession for sale any fruit packed in a closed package, upon which package is marked any designation which represents such fruit as of first, best or extra good quality, unless such fruit consists of well-grown specimens of one variety, sound, of nearly uniform size, of good colour for the variety, of normal shape, and not less than 90 per cent free from scab, worm holes, bruises and other defects, and properly packed. This is practically the same as clause No. <i, the only change being this description in place of the brand there indicated : 'Any designation which represents such fruit as of first, best or extra good quality.'
If any one should brand his fruit 1 Nova Scotia No. 1 ' or ' A No. 1,' that fruit would still come under the definition I have just given. If the insertion of such a clause will prevent any desire to amend clause No. (5, we can leave that clause as it is, in the hojfe that the people at large will gradually adopt the national brand described in clause 6, with its standard definition or description.

That is carrying out the suggestion 1 made on Friday. 1 suggested that it would be desirable to have a general definition of No. 1 apple, such as is given to No. 1 Canadian in clause 6. The difficulty I saw in the Bill as originally drafted was that a Nova Scotian need not use the brand ' No. 1 Canadian,' but none the less the apple-growers of that province desire that there should be some standard.
If this amendment be adopted, I shall withdraw the objection to clauses 6 and 7.

Is the hon. gentleman willing that there should be one standard for all Canada ? According to the hon. member for Annapolis (Mr. Wade) the description of a standard as ' Canadian ' would discredit Canadian apples.
-Mr. WADE. No.

Then why does the hon. gentleman say that if the Nova Scotians were to adopt a Canadian standard, that would throw discredit on their apples ? Nova Scotia would, in no sense be lost in the word ' Canada.' As Canadians, and legislating for the whole country, it is our duty to do all we can to place the name of Canada in the best light before the purchasers of our goods in England. If there are portions of Canada that are able to stand out and maintain a reputation of their own, I have no objection; but I do object to having an inferior standard for Canada and giving a special standard to Nova Scotia.
Is there anything in the Bill that would prevent growers in other provinces marking their apples ' N. S.' ?
No.

I do not think it is necessary to discuss the merits of the apjjles in the several provinces. Owing to climatic reasons, the crop may be better in Nova Scotia than in Ontario, but last year it was better in Ontario than in Nova Scotia. But what has been more particularly considered in Nova Scotia than in Ontario is honesty in packing. The Nova Scotia shippers have realized that to obtain a good market there must be honest packing ; and that is the secret of our apple trade. Let'the inferior qualities be disposed of for what they will bring, but let the best qualities only be shipped. The packers in Nova Scotia are very anxious to retain the advantage of the good name they have won on the London market, and I think they will not be satisfied unless there is a distinguishing mark by which their apples shall be known in that market.
I object, equally with the hon. member for Bothwell (Mr. Clancy) to this Bill passing without the provision that the word ' Canada' shall be on each barrel.
I have withdrawn my objection to the word ' Canadian' staying on.
As this Bill is not intended to provide compulsory branding for the barrels, it seems to me we are spending more time on it than it is worth.

We have spent two whole afternoons on it, and when it is passed it may not amount to a wave of your hand with respect to the branding of the barrels. The gist of the Bill is to provide that when the barrel is branded ' A No. T Canadian,' the apples in the barrel shall conform to a certain standard. So long as the Bill is not compulsory, it seems to me that the use of names such as 'Canadian,' ' Nova Scotia,' ' Ontario,' and others indicating locality will have to be left with the growers and1 exporters themselves. You do not compel them to put on any one of these words, but the intention is to compel them, if they put the words 'A No. 1 ' on the barrel, to put a certain class of apples in the barrel. If you leave out these words indicating locality, you will accomplish the result, for when the words ' A No. 1' appear on the barrel, we shall know that the contents of the barrel are up to a certain standard. That being the case, why not confine it to that, and deal with it in that sense in which the hon. gentleman (Hon,, Mr. Fisher) proposed to deal with it in his amendment ? All you need to do is to provide that the words 'A No. 1' or 1 extra quality ' or certain other words shall indicate a certain standard. If this is provided, you have the gist of the Bill, and you can leave out the consideration of such words as ' Canadian' and ' Nova Scotia.' I make this suggestion to hon. gentlemen who have been discussing the merits of the fruits of the different provinces. There is no objection to Nova Scotians putting the words ' Nova Scotia ' on their barrels if they see fit, and the same liberty will be allowed to other provinces. All we need to provide is that a certain mark on the barrel shall mean a certain quality of contents.
My hon. friend (Mr. Borden, Halifax) has spoken far too strongly in saying that that is the gist of the whole Bill. There are several parts of the Bill to which he lias not alluded.
Of course, I was referring to this feature of the Bill.

As to this feature, I stated frankly that sections 6 and 7 were a suggestion of what I hoped would be a national brand of Canadian fruit, which, I trusted, in. the course of time would become a well known brand with a reputation which would be a matter of pride for all Canadians. These clauses are not compulsory, for the reasons which I have already given, I shall be sorry, however, to eliminate these two clauses from the Bill, because I think in so doing we should throw away the opportunity we have of establishing that important feature of a national brand. A clause which has been suggested will cover the cases where these words are not used, and, that being the
case, I think the whole field is covered. And, if the committee will accept Nos. 6 and 7 I would like to move the insertion of No. 8 which I have proposed.
Mr. LaRIVIERE. Before accepting section 6, I would suggest the addition of the words ' for home market and export.' I do not see why we should exclude the home market and provide these amendments for the export trade alone. The home market needs protection as much as does the export market.

It seems to me there is a good deal of hair-splitting in connection with this Bill in order to adapt it to the peculiar conditions of Nova Scotia. The people of Ontario are as jealous of the reputation of their fruit as are the people of Nova Scotia of theirs. It seems to me that sections 6 and 7, as originally drafted, provide for the export business of the whole Dominion, and that there is no more reason for putting in a special clause to adapt the measure to the peculiar circumstances of Nova Scotia than there is for us to adapt it to the circumstances of Ontario or Quebec.

Before sections 6 and 7 and the proposed new clause are carried, I wish to call attention to one feature of the matter. The packer may sell his apples to a second person, and that second person to a third person, who may never have seen them. This occurs often in the trade. Yet the purchaser is held responsible for the packing, though it is the packer who has done wrotg in the first place. I think that is severe. I would not like to buy apples in that way. I have bought apples myself, and I have never seen the barrels, and would not like to be called upon and be fined for something that I did not know anything about, to be fined, in fact, for having been duped, as it were. I suggest that these words be added in clause 6 : ' No person shall with his knowledge sell or offer.'

I hardly think it possible to accept that amendment. These clauses were thoroughly discussed by the shippers, packers and fruit-growers, and they asked especially that they should appear in this form in the Bill. No such difficulties were felt to be likely by them. The innocent party would have recourse against the person who had deceived him. It is the packer who is liable, and the packer can be prosecuted by anybody who is aggrieved.

I think the suggestion made by the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. LaHiviore) is a very good one, with reference to inserting the statement that they are for export and home consumption. When we buy apples from the west we have great difficulty in getting as good fruit as the fruit which is exported. The fruitgrowers wish to send their finest fruit to

the old country, and they think anything is good enough for the rest of us Canadians. Now, we think we are entitled to have just as good fruit as people in the old country.

There is one point which I think has been overlooked by the Minister of Agriculture. Apples grown in Nova Scotia, or in Ontario, or in any other part of Canada, will have to find, the majority of them, a foreign market. We have been told that the North-west will become a great market for apples grown in Ontario. Now, the person who purchases the apples either in England or the Northwest will discover, in opening the barrels, that they are not up to the standard. The person discovering this will perhaps be a thousand miles distant from the packer, and in order to lodge an information and bring the packer to justice it seems to me he will be labouring under great difficulties. I think a clause should be added in the Bill something like this :
Whenever any barrel or package of apples shall be found to be in violation of this Act or any of its clauses, on information being laid before a justice of the peace or a judge in the district in which the apples are found to be bad in any country, an affidavit shall be made by not less than three persons of the fact, when such affidavit shall be forwarded under seal to the judge of the county or district in which the apple-packers reside; and said judge or magistrate shall have power to proceed under this Act, and a conviction may follow.
I think that clause should be introduced in this Bill, because I am satisfied that otherwise you will scarcely ever get a conviction. No man will come from Manitoba here to prosecute these gentlemen, it will cost him more than a cart-load of apples : and no one will come from England. So the law will be a dead letter unless you make some arrangement to prosecute these men.

I do not wish to take exception to clause 6 as standing by itself, but it needs to be considered along with other clauses. Now, there is nothing compulsory in the Bill, as I understand it, but the fourth clause. Clause 4 makes it imperative that the initials of the Christian name and surname and the address of the packer be put on the package, with the name and variety, and with the designation of the grade of fruit. That designation of the grade is also optional as I understand it.
Section 4 is imperative.

I am now discussing that part of clause 4 which is entirely optional, namely, with regard to the grade. With regard to the grade, any person may fix his own grade, because there is no grade fixed in the Bill. It is therefore optional, and every person may fix just such grade

by way of mark as be thinks proper. Then clause 6 and 7 are optional. Then we come to clause 8, which provides the penalties, It seems to me there is not much encouragement for a national standard, because a national standard is entirely optional. I think the Minister of Agriculture will concede that if we are to attempt a national standard we ought to adopt some moderate means of enforcing it. If we cannot hope to enforce a reasonable national standard, let us not deceive ourselves, and abandon the attempt. Otherwise I think it is mere child's play to put that in an Act of parliament when we know perfectly well that whenever It suits any person to abandon it they will do so. Now, we are putting a standard upon the statute-book with which nobody is compelled to comply. I still think that before we pass this clause 6 we should understand what the purpose of this Bill is. If the word ' Canadian ' is to he maintained at all, let it be maintained for all of the provinces, each being compelled to use that to designate the national standard. ' Nova Scotia No. 1, Canada,' would comply with the national standard, but it shows that the fruit came from a particular province. Fruit that is branded ' No. 1 Quebec, Canada,' is also of national standard. I mention this because it seems to be so necessary if we ever hope to maintain the Canadian position that we ought to take that course. It does seem to leave it optional and fix the standard as easily as one could well imagine. I hope the hon. Minister of Agriculture will insist on not multiplying clauses to overcome the difficulty, because, although I am not a lawyer, and therefore perhaps unable to clearly grasp the meaning of the section, it does seem to me that a multiplication of sections simply has a tendency to confuse matters. I would be willing to adopt the suggestion made by the hon. leader of the opposition, namely, that if it were necessary to mark apples ' No. 1,' let each province mark their own apples under the standard of No. 1, and make it compulsory to live up to that standard. I think that would meet the difficulty to a large extent.

If the lion. Minister of Agriculture does not make the use of the word ' Canadian ' compulsory, what office does section 6 fill, which is not filled by the section which he proposes to add ? It fills no office at all. If you add that section but do not make the use of the word ' Canadian ' compulsory, section 6 fills no office which would not he filled by the section which the hon. gentleman proposes to add. because, having regard to the section, if any person used the word ' Canadian,' which he might or might not, as lie saw fit, he would he liable to any penalty under the proposed section, which he would be liable to under section 6. It does not seem to be necessary to have the two sec-

tions in the Bill. You might as well eliminate section 6 and rely on the section which you propose to add.
Mr. LaRIVIERE. Yes, I would suggest that the minister erase the words ' intended for export.'

I simply propose this to encourage the establishment of the national brand. I may say that this section and the words in. it were proposed by the fruit-growers and shippers, and they have been asked for by every fruit-growers' association in this Dominion.

But it is rather a new idea to make suggestions by legislation. Legislation is supposed to mean something, and the hon, gentleman's legislation will mean something, namely, that the fruit inside a barrel must correspond with the brand on the outside of the barrel. Section 6 adds nothing at all to that beyond suggestion. I do not know whether I make myself clear to the hon. member for Annapolis (Mr. Wade).
I could not quite hear you.

I say that the hon. Minister of Agriculture proposes to add a section which says that fruit marked ' No. 1,' or designating other marks which he suggests, must be up to a certain standard, namely, the standard set forth in section 6. If you have that section, and do not make ,the use of the word ' Canadian ' compulsory, there is nothing in section 6 which is not carried out by the proposed section. Do I make myself clear to the hon. member for Annapolis ?
I understand you.

Therefore, it seems to me that section (5 is absolutely useless except as the hon. Minister of Agriculture says, it may be a suggestion to the fruit-growers throughout the country that they had better proceed to use the word ' Canadian.' Whether it is worth while to insert a section simply to make a suggestion is another question.

I may say that I consider it educational in leading up to a point which we all acknowledge is desirable. If we made it compulsory it would seriously interfere with and hamper trade, and therefore, I do not wish to make it compulsory, although I think it desirable.
Does the hon. Minister of Agriculture intend to appoint inspectors to inspect the apples ?

Yes
Mr. LaRIVIERE. Did you take out the words ' intended for export.'
Would you propose that ?

Yes, strike out the words ' intended for export.'
Section, as amended, agreed to.
On section 7,
Mr. BORDEN,(Halifax). In respect to the suggestion made by the hon. member for Middlesex (Mr. Gilmour), I think there is a good deal in it, but its consideration will come up perhaps more properly under section 12. I think it will then require serious consideration.
Mr. LaRIVIERE. I would propose that the words ' intended for export ' be struck out.
Section, as amended, agreed to.
On section S,

Section S is entirely different. I wish to substitute for this clause the following :
No person shall sell, or offer, expose or have in his possession for sale any fruit packed in a closed package, upon which package is marked any designation which represents such fruit as of first, best or extra good quality, unless such fruit consists of well-grown specimens of one variety, sound, of nearly uniform size, of good colour for the variety, of normal shape, and not less than 90 per cent free from scab, worm holes, bruises and other defects, properly packed.
This is the designation of clause No. 6, except iu the designation which represents the fruit as being of first, best, or extra good quality.
Section, as amended, agreed to.

I wish to insert here another clause which will cover part of clause S. It is as follows :
No person shall sell, or offer, or expose, or have in his possession for sale any fruit packed in any package in which the face or shown surface gives a false representation of the conditions of such package, and it shall be considered false representation when more than 15 per cent of such fruit is substantially smaller in size than, or inferior in grade to, or different in variety from the face or shown surface of such package.
That is with reference to the portion of clause 8 which does not deal with the grade but applies to the requirements which forces the packer to put his good fruit in the middle of the package as he does at the ends.
Mr. LaRIVIERE. There is a fraud often committed by the middlemen by which barrels are sometimes opened and an inferior fruit is substituted. As it is now, the packer is responsible, but if the middleman interferes the packer should be protected against him and a heavy penalty should be inflicted.

The person who offers it for sale is equally liable with the packer.
Mi'. LaRIYIERE. That is if the article is inferior, but suppose he sells it just as he got it from the packer ?

He is still apparently liable.
Mr. LaRIYIERE. The packer ought to be protected against the iniddleman who would substitute inferior fruit.

YYe can deal with that in another clause.
Mr. LaRIYIERE. That will be satisfactory.
On section 9,

What is the intention of the minister with respect to the suggestion of the hon. member for Middlesex (Mr. Gilmour), who referred to the supposed case of a barrel of apples packed in violation of this Act, they being properly No. 3, whereas they were packed and branded as No. 1, and that barrel passing into the hands of an innocent person who believes it is all right and sells it without any guilty intention. Do you propose by this Act to render him liable to a fine or imprisonment ?
Fine.

He could be imprisoned if he did not pay the fine. There are many statutes which are applicable only to persons who wilfully and knowingly violate the law. What is the intention with regard to this Act 1

I may say to my hon. friend (Mr. Borden, Halifax) who is a lawyer and who would know more about it than I do, that the intention was to make the person who sold the package liable. Take the conditions in the province of Manitoba, which my hon. friend from Pro-vencher (Mr. LaRiviSre) has so ably represented here. The merchant in Winnipeg who buys fruit from Ontario would be held responsible by his customers, and he would have recourse against the person from whom he bought in Ontario. The ordinary purchaser would be powerless against the original packer, but the merchant engaged in the trade would be sufficiently interested to follow him up. If we were to make only the original packer responsible we would practically destroy the value of the Act for the protection of the ordinary purchaser.

I see a very strong objection to punishing a person under the law for an act which he does not wilfully do, and for which he is not responsible.
Mr. LaRIYIERE.
Grain is sold subject to inspection, and these apples should be inspected before you buy them from the first party. If you buy them subject to inspection you take no risk.

If this law makes the second handler of the apples responsible it will drive men out of the business. They cannot look into every barrel of apples they buy to see that it is all right. 1 do not think it is fair to punish men for what they may not be responsible for.

Some statutes impose a penalty upon persons who have no guilty intention, and some statutes require the guilty intention. You should have it made perfectly plain in this Act as to which is intended. My own view is that the person subject to the provisions of this statute should be a person who wilfully violates the provisions of the Act, and you should not make it applicable to the case suggested by my hon. friend from Middlesex (Mr. Gilmour).
You might say negligently or wilfully.

If you like you may put the burden of proof on the person who sells the apples to show that he was not guilty of fraud. But to impose a penalty of this character upon a person who is guilty of no intention to violate the Act or of negligence which might amount to an intention, seems to me to be going beyond any necessity in the public interest, and might lead to very grave injustice ; and for my part I would oppose carrying this Act that far. I am prepared to support the framing of the Act so that a person selling such apples must prove that he did so innocently, and that he was not guilty of negligence or recklessness in doing so. Without that the Act might become inoperative ; but to say that a person who was absolutely innocent of any intention or negligence in such a matter, should be liable to this penalty, would be going beyond what is usual in statutes of this kind.

It seems to me that if a man undertakes to buy and sell again, it is his duty to see that the goods which he undertakes to sell are up to the standard of the marks upon them ; and if he sells the goods in ignorance of their quality, it is a dereliction of duty to his customer, for which he should be punished. If the word ' knowingly ' or ' intentionally ' were inserted in this section, it would nullify the whole Act, and the public whom we are trying to protect would be open to the same frauds as they have been in times past.

Take the case of fish, which are branded No. 1, No. 2 and No. 3. The inspector is held responsible

in every instance ; and if the fish turn out, even in the market of the United States, not to be as represented, he is subject to a penalty. If you are going to appoint an inspector, I think he is the man who should be held responsible for the quality of the apples, and no one else.
How can an inspector inspect a hundred barrels of apples ? He simply puts his mark on them, and he cannot tell whether they are up to the standard without examining each barrel.

It is not intended to attempt to have a universal inspection of fruit. Inspectors will be appointed who may possibly inspect ; and should they inspect any apples and find them wrongly marked, it will be their duty to prosecute the people so marking them. But there is going to be no attempt to make a universal inspection.

I cannot understand what good the inspector would be at all. In the county of Kent it would take twenty-five inspectors to inspect the fruit shipped out of one township. A thousand barrels are packed in a day.

In regard to the inspection of fruit, the system that prevails in California will have to be adopted in this country. You will have to have smaller packages and hand-pack your fruit; and it will have to be packed in boxes in such a way that every single piece of fruit can be seen. The apple barrel will have to go, and the sooner our Canadian fruit shippers understand that the better it will be for the fruit trade. The fruit-growers of California have a market all over the continent, which has been built up by giving the greatest attention to the packing of the fruit and the maintaining of its quality. We shall have to come to the same thing in Canada, whether by law or otherwise. I would like to know how that is secured in California-whether by the interference of the state law or by the people who are engaged in the trade coming to see that it is the only way to get and maintain a market.

When the apples cannot all be inspected, I cannot see of what use the inspection will be. An inspector will brand a lot of barrels without having inspected them at all. I would like to have it provided that every barrel shall be inspected by the inspector before he puts his name on it.
There is no intention that the inspector shall put his name on any of them.

With respect to the inspection of fruit in the United States, 77
prunes, for instance, are not inspected by a government inspector, but by the person who packs them. The prunes put up by Giffen & Skelly are put up in packages of uniform size, and marked from 60 to 70, from 70 to SO, from 80 to 90, and from 90 to 100. That means that there are that many prunes in a pound ; so that you know exactly what you are buying. In the same way oranges are put up in packages marked 400, 500 or 600, according to the number in each jiackage; and the name of the packer is put on the package, so that the purchaser knows against whom he has recourse.
On section 10,

I think the House should have some expression from the Minister of Agriculture as to how far he intends to saddle inspectors upon the public service. It seems to me that the inspection will be a farce unless we have some defined limits placed upon it; for it would be utterly impossible to warrant the expense of a complete inspection in a matter of this kind. I would like the minister to state how many inspectors he intends to appoint, where they will be stationed, and generally what will be expected of them. The hon. gentleman increased his difficulties when he assented to the proposition made by the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. La Riviere), namely, that all apples packed, whether for export or for domestic use, will come under the same rules and require the same inspection.

While the Bill permits inspection, there is no expectation or intention that any attempt shall be made to inspect all the fruit packed for trade in Canada or for export. I have investigated that matter pretty fully, I have discussed it with exporters, shippers and fruit-growers in all parts of the country, and 1 believe it would be a physical impossibility for any number of inspectors who could be appointed by a government or called for by this House to accomplish that result. When a Bill of this kind becomes law, it will be necessary to appoint some inspector. Otherwise we would throw upon the purchaser the necessity for protecting himself. In the interior trade, he can do that very well. If a purchaser finds he is being defrauded, he can, under the provisions of this Act, attack the seller. But in the export trade the case is different, and in order to protect the good name of Canada and improve the reputation of our fruit abroad, I think we should have a few inspectors at the ports of export. This is purely a deterrent provision, and not one which we expect to be exercised in every instance or even in the majority of instances. But the shippers and packers will know that their goods are liable to be inspected at any time. It will be necessary to have



two or three men at Montreal, who will proceed against any shipper whom they may And violating this Act. In Nova Scotia it will also be necessary to have two or three inspectors. There is a large amount of fruit packed in the different parts of Ontario and Quebec which is shipped to Montreal. A good many packers would like to have their fruit inspected before shipping, so that it would not be opened at Montreal, and it may be necessary to have a certain number of men on call who could go to the warehouses of the packers and inspect the fruit and mark it before it leaves. I could not give the exact number of inspectors required, but I suppose there would be ten or a dozen appointed this coming fall, and If necessary to appoint more, they could be appointed later.

I do not see any objection to having inspectors at the points of shipment because we must protect the good name of Canada as far as i>ossible, but I do see serious objection to appointing emergency inspectors-men who may be called on at any moment to inspect at the warehouses. To give any government the power of appointing as many inspectors as it chooses would be very dangerous and open to abuse. The hon. gentleman knows the pressure that will always be used by skippers and others, who will not want their fruit disturbed at Montreal, to have it inspected before shipment, and this will give ample opportunity for the exercise of favouritism.

I agree with the hon. member for Bothwell (Mr. Clancy). I do not see why inspectors should be appointed all over the Dominion. I would move that clause 10 be amended by adding thereto :
Inspectors may be appointed at the ports of export.
These words will begin the clause and the rest of the clause will be the same as in the Bill.

I do not think that would work. The fruit-growers themselves are very earnestly requesting that all the inspection should not Tie done at the port of export. There is no danger that the large number of inspectors will be appointed which the hon. member for Bothwell seems to anticipate. It will be physically impossible to meet the view of all shippers, and therefore it is not at all likely that certain favoured ones will be picked out and be given the privilege of having their fruit inspected before shipment to the ports of export. At the same time, there is an internal trade to be more or less watched and guarded, though not to the same extent as the export trade. Further, if the inspectors are to do their work at the port of Montreal only, they cannot do it as effectively as they should. The hon. gen-

tleman may not have been at the port of Montreal during the apple shipping season, but there are sometimes a hundred thousand barrels in the port being shipped and awaiting shipment. It would be quite impossible, under that condition of affairs for even three or four inspectors in the port to do their work in such a way as to be really deterrent to the packer. I think we must count upon occasionally dropping on a shipment of fruit elsewhere than in the port of shipment. And, if we have not inspectors available for that purpose, we would, to a certain extent, not fulfil the expectations of the shippers, the growers or the public.
These inspectors are only to be temporarily employed ?
During the fruit season, yes.

There are other ports besides Montreal, such as Halifax, St. John, Toronto and Niagara-for fruit goes by way of New York as well as by Montreal. Even though there were a hundred thousand barrels, additional inspectors could be appointed to meet the case. As to the terminal trade, if the barrels are marked falsely, the person who has them for sale is liable to a fine. Therefore, I cannot see the object of having inspectors in any other place than the points where the apples leave this country. If a Canadian has his barrels marked wrongly, he deserves to suffer the loss of freight or even to have the fruit confiscated at Montreal. The port of export, where the barrels are all collected, is the proper place for inspection, and I cannot see the object of having inspection elsewhere.

I cannot accept the amendment, because I think it can only hamper the working of the Act. I think it is desirable and necessary to have inspectors available to do work at such points as may be desired.
How do you propose to pay the inspectors ?

By salary-monthly payments. As the inspection is permissive, I do not think it would be wise to have a fee, in fact, I think it would be impossible.
Amendment negatived.
On section 15,

This section refers to an appeal from conviction under this Act. If, upon appeal, the apples were held during the consideration of the case, damage would naturally result. If the appeal should be sustained is there any provision for indemnifying the man who has thus suffered from damage ?

I could not say whether it is usual for per-

ishable goods to be held during such a trial or not.
But I would ask the min-istef to consider that point.

I should suppose that evidence would be taken as to the condition of the fruit and that evidence would have to be submitted on appeal. But, not being a lawyer I cannot give an opinion on such a matter.
On section 16,

I hope the Minister of Agriculture will not insist on this clause as it stands. If there is anything more dangerous than another, it is to encourage the class of men who live on blood-money. I am sure the Minister of Agriculture will see how a crop of abuses would arise if you offer inducement to men who inform for the money alone. In order to close the discussion, I move that all the words after the words ' be payable to His Majesty ' be struck out, and that the clause should read this way : ' Any fine or penalty imposed under this Act shall, when recovered, be payable to His Majesty.' I am sure the Minister of Agriculture will concur in the statement tha.t to encourage, in matters of that kind, persons to become informers by giving them one-half the fine, is a mistaken policy. The hon. gentleman -frill find that the Act will be better observed by making it a common interest, than to hold out inducements to a class of persons by offering them a share' of the fine. Paying fines to any persons as informers is to my mind an unsound principle.

I am in entire accord with the hon. member for Bothwell (Mr. Clancy). It is the most objectionable clause in the whole Bill, and I hope the minister will see his way to amend it. I can imagine that much wrong will be done under this clause.

This clause is simply following the principle adopted in many other Acts. For instance, in the license law there is a clause of this kind, in the Scott Act there is a clause of this kind, in the law regarding the seizure of tobacco there is a clause of this kind, as well as in many other laws. I do not think' it would be worth while now to change this principle, because it is an admitted principle in our legislation. It may have objectionable features, and in certain instances may be abused ; still on the whole it has worked fairly well during a long term of jurisprudence.

The cases the hon. gentleman has cited are not parallel. The case regarding infractions of the revenue is entirely different. I could picture a man going about the country making case after case. The hon. gentleman knows that under the Scott Act and under our license system 77i
we have found the greatest evils arising from men endeavouring to make a living from fines. A class of professional informers has arisen that go about the country. If a man informs for the purpose of getting a fine he is not informing in the public interest, he is bound to hunt up and to trump up some charge for the purpose of making money out of it. I hope the hon. gentleman will not import that objectionable feature into his Bill. If he makes that law, he will find it one of the most objectionable laws that has ever been passed by this House. The Bill has been made wider by adopting the proposal of the hon. member for Proveneher, and will expose the whole farming community of Canada to these penalties and to these penalty hunters.

The Solicitor General (Hon. Mr. Fitzpatrick) has pointed out section 25 of the General Inspection Act, which has been in existence for a great many years, over a hundred I think. It is an admitted principle of our jurisprudence.

I tell the hon. gentleman that when the proper stage arrives I shall divide the House on this feature of the Bill.
On section 3,

We will have to go back to section 3, which I was asked to allow to stand on Friday. My hon. friend from South Wentworth (Mr. Smith) requested me to make some modification in the definition of a closed package. After carefully considering the matter and discussing it with my officers, I have decided to propose this change in the lines of the hon. gentleman's request:
Closed package means a box or barrel, of which the contents cannot be seen or inspected when such package is closed.
It was not intended that this word ' closed package ' should apply to small baskets used for selling small fruit, because they are really open packages in the sense that the cover is so easily removed.
What about a crate ?

A crate, I think, would not be a closed package under the definition I have suggested. The hon. member for South Wentworth did not wish a crate to be included.
Section as amended, agreed to.
The minister, perhaps, has forgotten that section. 2 has not been passed yet.

I think there is no question about the date. I think it would be a great misfortune if we did not put the law into operation for the fruit season of the present year. I must ask that the clause be adopted.
Bill reported.

The MINISTER OP MARINE AND FISHERIES (Hon. Sir Louis Davies) moved second reading of Bill (No. 91) to amend the Inland Waters Seamen's Act.
Motion agreed to, Bill read the second time; and House went into committee thereon.
On section 1,

This Bill is one simply to define more accurately the expression ' Inland waters of Canada ' which, as the statute now stands, are defined to be the inland waters above the harbour of Quebec. That has been found to be too vague. The intention is to make the definition embrace what are really the inland waters of Canada.
speakername: The MINISTER OP MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: It does not seem that it is quite definite enough in regard to the sea coast. For example, what would the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Sir Louis Davies) think about the Bras d'Or lakes which are arms of the sea really ?
They are defined clearly in the main Act. There is no doubt about those.
speakername: The MINISTER OP MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
What about the arms of the sea V
The	MINISTER	OF	MARINE	AND
FISHERIES. They are ail defined to be the sea coast.

Has the hon. gentleman the statute there which defines that ? I would like to see it.
The	MINISTER	OP	MARINE	AND
FISHERIES. Yes.

While the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries is looking that up, I would like to ask him what his views are on this point :
The expression ' inland waters of Canada ' includes all the river3, lakes and other navigable waters within Canada.
Of course that implies that this section only includes the navigable	rivers and	lakes.
Is that the meaning that the hon. minister puts upon it ? It would hardly be intended to apply to those inland waters and lakes that are now navigable.
The	'MINISTER	OP	MARINE	AND
FISHERIES. The Revised Statutes, chap. 75, which relates to the shipping of seamen on inland waters, defines inland waters in subsection f of section 2 as follows :
The expression ' ship subject to the provisions of this Act' includes every ship registered in Canada propelled by steam and of more than twenty tons registered tonnage, or propelled otherwise

than by steam and of more than fifty tons registered tonnage, and employed in navigating the inland waters of Canada above the harbour of Quebec.
Now, the question was, what were the inland waters above the harbour of Quebec 7 Did they extend to the great * lakes and rivers ? In order to relieve the ambiguity we define the words ' inland waters ' to include all the

Rivers, lakes and other navigable waters within Canada, except salt water bays and gulfs on the sea coast, and includes the River St. Lawrence so far seaward as a line drawn from Cape Chatte on the south shore to Point des Monze on the north shore.
The reason that point was selected was, that in the reciprocity treaty between Great Britain and the United States, that was the point selected internationally as the mouth of the River St. Lawrence, and so we took that international definition as a reasonable one to import into this Bill, defining all within that point to be inland waters.

I would like to ask the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Sir Lillis Davies) if this makes any difference in the provisions or working of the Act relating to shipping through the St. Lawrence and on the great lakes ?
It only makes clear that the upper waters of the great lakes are the inland waters of Canada, which was in doubt before.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: There would be a question about the so-called lakes, Bras d'Or lakes, for Instance, which are really arms of the sea. There might also be a question about arms of the sea on the coast of Nova Scotia. They might not technically be called bays or gulfs. Would it not be better to insert ' Salt water arms of the sea.'

I shall be glad to insert ' arms of the sea ' If necessary.
Section as amended agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time, and passed.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES moved second reading of Bill (No. 92) further to amend the Act respecting the safety of ships.
Motion agreed to, Bill read the second time ; and House resolved itself Into committee thereon.
(In the Committee.)
On section 1,

This Bill simply makes an

alteration in the present law to bring it into conformity with the British statute. I propose to re-enact the whole section, putting in the alteration which is confined to subsection d. Since the original Act was passed large steel steamships having much permanently covered in space have been introduced, and by our statute you are only allowed to place deals in this covered in space to a height of three feet from the deck, the rest of the space remaining vacant. By the Imperial law they are allowed to place a light class of goods in this space which is now left vacant according to our law. The shipping interests are under a disadvantage in this. They consider it is a serious grievance, and it is proposed to amend the Act by permitting the carriage in covered in spaces of :	.
Any deals, battens or other lightwood goods, of any description to a height not exceeding three feet above the deck in any space where the deck of such ship is closed in.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: This restricts them from filling in the remaining part of the space with deals.

speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
This does not interfere with the shipping of deals to South America or coast wise.
The	MINISTER	OF	MARINE	AND
FISHERIES. I do not alter the law in that respect at all. This refers simply to deals going to Great Britain.

Does it change the law as regards the tliree-feet limit on the open deck ?
The	MINISTER	OF	MARINE	AND
FISHERIES. Not in any respect.

Has the hon. minister any opinion on that point ?
The	MINISTER	OF	MARINE	AND
FISHERIES. I have a very strong opinion. After consulting with the trade and getting the opinion of the best expert officers, I came to the conclusion that it was safer in every respect to allow vessels to fill with deal flush to the bulwark. I urged that very strongly upon the board of trade in England, and the Hon. Mr. Dobell personally urged them to agree to that, but they
did not see their way clear to do it, and therefore there is no use in our doing it.
I pointed out to the board of trade the reasons why our shippers thought it would be better not to limit it to three feet from the deck, because a kind of well was formed in which the water moved backward and forward, whereas if the cargo was flush with the deck it would wash off. The English Board of Trade is very slow and conservative, and they did not see their way to adopt the suggestion. My hon. friend (Mr. Calvin) will see that it is absolutely essential we should bring our law into exact conformity with the English law.

I quite see that. I would like to read a statement I received from a firm of very long standing with regard to this matter. The letter is of considerable length, but I shall only read a short extract from it which is in line with what the hon. minister has said. It is from Messrs. Henry Fry & Co. of Quebec. They say :
Having been connected with the management of ships for over forty years, we are aware that when the deck-load law was inaugurated it principally applied to sailing vessels carrying such cargo on open decks; but we were always of opinion that limiting the deck-load to a height of three feet was a mistake,, when connected with sailing vessels or steamers having bulwarks. These should be allowed to carry deckload level with their rail, as this would constitute equal to a flush deck, over which the sea would readily pass, whereas with only three feet deck cargo, it is frequently below the level of rail and forms a well for the reception of seas, which float and dislodge the cargo at great risk of life and property.

I thoroughly agree with that, and in point of fact I drafted a Bill in that sense, and intimated to the Board of Trade of England that I wished to bring in, a Bill in that sense; but they did not see their way to agree to it, and there is no use of our doing it until they do agree.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I think the word ' enacted ' in the third line of section 1 must he meant for the word ' amended.' Would the hon. gentleman be good enough to tell me what his idea is of the office of these words in the section as it originally appears in the revised statutes : ' and during the voyage while within Canadian jurisdiction.'' Taking these words in connection with the context, either I do not understand them, or else there should be a change.

Of course. I am not responsible for the phraseology; and, as the Act has been a long time on the statute-book, I did not care to amend it. The object is this. A vessel sailing from a port in Canada might have the cargo all right when she started; but before she left the jurisdiction of Canada, she might alter it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: That was my own idea of the meaning, and it seemed to me that the word ' or ' should be used instead of the word ' and.'
I will be glad to accept those suggestions of the hon. gentleman.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I think the word ' and ' is correct.

Suppose a vessel started from Montreal all right, and put on some more cargo at Quebec. If the word ' and ' was there, she would not necessarily break the law, because she did not do it from the port of starting. It seems to me that the word ' or ' carries out the intention of the Act-that a vessel shall not do it either at the port from which she starts, or at any time after she starts and while she is in Canadian jurisdiction.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I think the language is quite correct as it is. The intention of the section is, while a ship sailing from one place to another and while within Canadian jurisdiction. Therefore the word 'and' is the only proper word.

As there is a difference among lawyers, we will stand by the old law.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES (Sir Louis Davies) moved second reading of Bill (No. 93) respecting inquiries and investigations into shipping casualties.
He said: The'object of this Bill is to meet a number of objections to the present system raised by the British government. At present the inquiries are undertaken at the request of merchants, shippers or others, and there are two kinds of inquiry. One is a preliminary inquiry to find out the cause of the disaster, and I do not propose to alter the character of that inquiry at all. Then a formal inquiry may be made, either after a preliminary inquiry or without one. In the old statute, the formal investigation is made at the instance of the Minister of Marine, who appoints a commissioner to investigate. The commissioner need not be a judicial officer, and generally is a sea captain supposed to bq an expert on nautical matters. But it by no means follows that such an expert is a good judicial officer capable of holding legal investigation. Our law enables us to hold investigations into casualties and punish officers holding certificates who are found guilty of laches or neglect, whether they hold British or Sir LOUIS DAVIES.
Canadian certificates. Such certificates may be taken from the officers convicted, either for a term or entirely*cancelled. The construction placed on the old statute by the Department of Justice was that the reports of these investigations could be revised on appeal by the Minister of Marine himself, who might lengthen the term of suspension of the certificate or entirely cancel the certificate. The British government, however, held that the Minister of Marine here had no power to cancel any certificate granted to a British officer. My predecessor and myself have always exercised that power and consequently there was a clash of jurisdiction. After a good deal of correspondence, I advised my colleagues that I thought it better to yield to the representations of the British government and not attempt to cancel the certificate of a British officer, even though the casualty happened to the ship in Canadian waters. An investigation is held by an officer appointed by us, and the evidence and the report of that officer are forwarded to the British Board of Trade.
Would the British authorities try and punish a Canadian captain for a casualty that happened in British waters ?
They claim jurisdiction in that regard over all officers.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: There ought to be reciprocity.

There are some things you cannot help. For instance, in the case of a ship lost in the Bay of Fundy, I cancelled, sitting as a court of appeal, the certificate of the captain, in conformity with the opinion of the Minister of Justice that I had the power to do so. But the British Crown officers held I had not.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Could you not argue that before the Privy Council ?

I do not see how I could. They contended strongly that our investigations should be made to partake of a judicial character the same as the British investigation, and where a man's position was at stake, they should be held as far as possible by a judicial officer. I propose to make a change in the selection of persons to hold such investigation by declaring that ' The minister may appoint any officer of the government of Canada, or any judge of the county court, or any judge of the superior court of the province of Quebec, or any stipendiary magistrate, to be a commissioner for the purpose of such investigation, and such commissioner shall be deemed a court for such purpose.' Along with the commissioner two nautical experts will be appointed to advise him. I will

point out in each section where the amendments are made. This Bill is the outcome of consultation with the British Board of Trade and the Department of Justice. It is satisfactory to the British Board of Trade and approved by the Department of Justice ; and sections are inserted to provide for the recovery of penalties under the code. With this general information I would suggest that we go through the sections in committee, and as we come to each one, I will explain what the proposed changes are.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Should not the cancellation of a master's certificate here be under the jurisdiction or judgment of a nautical expert instead of the department itself ?
I would suggest that we should deal with that point in committee. I can explain more fully when we come to the section covering that point.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
Motion agreed to, Bill read the second time, and House went into committee thereon.
On section 1,

Just one question, and if that is all right, I have no objection to the Bill. Supposing that we conform to the English practice and procedure, and appoint a judicial officer, will they acknowledge our right to cancel their certificates or not ?
No.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I do not like the indication from what the minister has said that he has surrendered a Canadian right without making a fight for it.
No, I did not.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Fracticaly, that is what the hon. gentleman said.
Wrong again.

No, I am not wrong. The hon. minister has surrendered a Canadian right without any proper effort to maintain it. This government has claimed that on several occasions they have vindicated Canadian rights, and they have claimed credit for it. Here is a very important matter affecting our shipping. I have known, in an off-hand kind of way, that the British authorities claimed jurisdiction over our shipping, and that we had not full control of it. I should be sorry if that is the case. But I would not be a party to surrendering any right possessed by Canada without fighting to the last ditch to retain it.
Hear, hear.

The Solicitor General evidently approves what I say. I have been trying to find out in what respect we come under their jurisdiction and law and are not in supreme control of our own affairs. If this is one of those cases, I, as a Canadian, object to a surrender being made until after every means has been exhausted to vindicate our rights in this matter.	[DOT]

It is merely a construction of the old statute. We held that that statute gave the minister power to deal with matter coming on appeal to him and relating to the certificates of the officers of vessels on which a casuality has occurred, and to deal with the officer holding a British certificate as well as with the officer holding a Canadian certificate. The Department of Justice held the view held by myself and my predecessor. But the Board of Trade of Great Britain decided that they would not hold our Act valid, and the British Crown law officers supported them in that. So, what could I do ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Has Canada no head of appeal from an arbitrary action of the British Board of Trade ?
I did not suppose that we were desirous of doing it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: We do not want to surrender anything.

But here is the position-we grant certificates to officers on ships, as captains, ns first officers, second officers and engineers. Nobody questions our right to cancel the certificate of any officer holding our certificate who commits an offence or is guilty of negligence. But if a British officer comes here and a casualty occurs to his ship, our statutes allows us to hold an investigation. We hold it, the court recommend that the captain's certificate be cancelled. Then you must send the evidence home, with a report of the court, and they say : If we concur in it, we will cancel the certificate.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Is not that reasonable ?

But take the converse of that. Suppose a Canadian officer is sailing in British waters and an accident happened, and the matter is tried by the officers of the British Admiralty-do they take away his certificate ? Or do they send back their finding for the confirmation or revision of the minister-have they admitted that ?
No.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Then, they have put Canada in an inferior position.
What clause is the hon. gentleman (Mr. Maclean) discussing ?
I am discussing the principle of the Bill.
X rise to a point of order-no clause of the Bill has been read.
I am perfectly in order, Mr. Chairman.	t
I want a ruling on that point.
I think that on the first clause the hon. gentleman can discuss that.

From what I gathered from the hon. minister's statement a Canadian officer can be disciplined in British waters, but a British officer cannot be disciplined in Canadian waters. Is that a fact or not ?
I wish to point out to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries that it would be well to make subsection e conform to the definition of ' inland waters ' in the Bill already passed, would it not ?

Yes.
On section 2,
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: It seems to me that the word ' coast ' should be defined in a manner to conform to the Act.
The phraseology is not the same, and if the hon. gentleman thinks we have expressions that are not equivalent we may change it. But I think the expression will be found all right.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I was going to suggest that the word should be added ' as defined by
I would rather make it complete in that Act. The question is : Have we embraced in the two expressions ' inland waters ' and ' coast ' all the waters in which a casualty might take place.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I do not think it is important only except for conformity.

I am willing to consider any suggestion, but it struck me that the two definitions in the Bill covered all that was necessary :
(e)	The expression ' inland waters ' includes all the rivers, lakes and other navigable waters within Canada ;
(f)	The expression 1 coasts ' includes the sea coast and the salt water bays, gulfs and harbours on the sea coast.
On section 3,
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: In this section the new part is in subsections e and f.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I would like to know whether, in this list of casualties is included damage to the canals of the Dominion. 1 think that the method employed at present of dealing with that sort of damage is most unfair to those using the canals. Now, the canals are built by the government. They may be good canals like the Soulanges canal, which was built by our friend Mr. Munro, or it tnay be a work with glaring defects, such as the Welland canal. I need not go into particulars, they may be shown by competent men who are using the canals. That is the condition as regards the construction of the works. Now as to the craft that use them. A steamer that goes through that canal, before she is allowed to turn a wheel, must have her hull inspected and her machinery inspected, and the same government that builds those canals makes her owners pay for the inspection. Then before she is allowed to proceed on her voyage she must be manned by a captain who has to receive and pay for a certificate of competency from this government, by a mate, who likewise has to obtain a certificate from the government and to pay for it, by an engineer and an assistant engineer who likewise have to receive certificates from the government and to pay for them; though indirectly it is, the owner of the vessel that has to pay for all that expense. The employees of the canal are the servants of the government. I do not know that they have to pass any examination or to pay any fee before they are appointed, I do not think they do. Those are the circumstances. Now a vessel damages a lock, or bridge, or some other portion of the government's property in the canal, the owner of that vessel is obliged to pay every dollar of expense at such prices as the government may name. He has nothing to do with the naming of the prices, he cannot go on and repair the work himself. He has to pay the government for every dollar of that work at their own prices, and without having an investigation.

I dare say the hon. gentleman may have some [DOT] ground of complaint as to the stringency of the law in that respect; but the present Act does not touch those cases at all.
-Mr. CALVIN. It ought to.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: That may be, but it does not come within the scope of the Marine Inquiries Act at all. The hon. gentleman speaks of a case where a ship going through the canal does some damage. 1 do not know what takes place there. An investigation is held in a court of law, I suppose. That does not come up here.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
I suppose if a vessel happened to be damaged in passing through the canal, that would be another thing.
On section S,

Under the old law you could appoint any commissioner or body corporate to hold an investigation. Now the minister may appoint any officer of the government of Canada, or any judge of the county court, or any judge of the Superior Court of the province of Quebec, or any stipendiary magistrate, to be commissioner. The object is to make the commissioner a judicial officer instead of a merely nautical expert. Subsection 2 of this section is new. It has been suggested by the Board of Trade so as to be in accord with the Merchant's Shipping Act. These are the exact words of the Merchant's Shipping Act which they advise us to incorporate in our own.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: The minister has omitted the new offence that he has put in section 8, that is, ' or has failed to render assistance and to give information.' That is not carried into subsection 2.

Subsection 1 gives authority to the minister to authorize this investigation to be held where he believes that any master, mate or engineer is from incompetency or misconduct unlit to discharge his duties, or has failed to render assistance, and to give any information in case of collision. Then the court so appointed is authorized to hold a formal investigation.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: In section 2 is there any power to inquire into a failure to render assistance and to give information ?
In order to make it conform with section 1, it would be better to add the words 1 where the minister has reason to believe.'

Subsection (e) meets the first suggestion my hon. friend made as to failing to render assistance or to give information. The first part of the section states the conditions under which you are authorized to initiate the inquiry, where you have reason to believe so and so. The other part follow's the Merchant's Shipping Act, I would not like to alter that.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
I do not see why the hon. minister uses the same expression
in one case and an entirely different expression in another case. In subsection 2 you say :
A court so appointed as aforesaid is authorized to hold a formal investigation.
Where a master has been charged with incompetency or misconduct. When you come down to subsections d and e you do not say where he is charged, but you say where he ' fails.' You do not say where he is charged with failing, but where he does fail.
I would suggest that I do not think this is so important as to desire a change, inasmuch as it follows the exact phraseology of the British Act.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I would like to understand from the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries, what would be the meaning of the word ' incompetency.' For instance, if an engineer were to make a mistake in the bell and if the vessel ran ashore that would be incompetency and his certificate would be taken away. Am I right in that ?

I would not like to enter upon a judicial interpretation of these words. The object of the Bill is to appoint a judicial officer to listen to the evidence and to decide such points after being advised by two experts.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Would the provisions of the Bill not apply to an accident in a canal as well as to one elsewhere ? If the engineer takes the wrong bell and an accident happens in a canal, or, if the captain is not doing his duty, or is under the influence of liquor, and an accident happens in the Welland, or in some other canal, would there be an investigation held and the certificate of the engineer or captain be taken away ? Why should the Bill not apply to this case ? You have never had any investigation yet into any accident that has happened on the Welland canal, and there are more accidents happening in the Welland canal than on any of the inland waters.

It may be a subject-matter deserving of consideration whether these merchant shipping inquiries should not apply to the navigation of the canals as well as to the navigable waters of Canada. So far it has not been deemed advisable to apply the provisions of the law to the canals. However, I shall take note of what the hon. gentleman suggests and talk it over with my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Blair).
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: If these accidents were included it would perhaps make
Perhaps it might get ns into more difficulties ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: No, no-it might make captains more careful, and in addition it would result in putting the blame where it really belongs.
I will consider that point.

speechtext: The owners of ships are placed in a peculiar position. When an investigation takes place there should be a marine expert appointed who is thoroughly versed in marine matters, and in that way the owner of the ship would have justice which he would not have otherwise.

Complaints were made by the captains, mates and others implicated that when the court held an investigation it did not render its decision in open court but perhaps delivered it in Halifax or some other place a fortnight afterwards. The captain or mate was not present and had no means of knowing what the decision was. It is claimed that the decision should be rendered in open court so that they may know what the decision is.

Where a certificate has been issued by the Dominion of Canada it may be dealt with by the minister, where it has been issued by the board of trade, it has to be forwarded with a report of the evidence to the board of trade, and where it has been issued by any British possession other than Canada it shall be sent to the Governor of such British possession. I suppose that other British possessions have similar enactments. What is the practice between ourselves and other British possessions in respect to the cancellation of such certificates ?

Other British possesions are governed by the provisions of the Imperial Act. That is most of them are-the Crown colonies. I do not remember that we have ever had any cases from Australia or the Cape. The British government will not accept our Canadian certificates unless we give them control over them, and as it is of greater importance that our certificates should be accepted than that we should retain exclusive control, we give them control.

Is not the section rather too comprehensive in its terms. An investigation may be commenced in the United Kingdom and may prove to be absolutely inoperative, because the witnesses may have come to Canada. Under this section you could not proceed with the inquiry in Canada.
I did not like to interfere with the phraseology of the Merchant's Shipping Act of which this is an exact copy.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: It seems to me to be very loosely drawn.
Do you mean the language of the Imperial Act ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
Yes. I do, because it seems to preclude an inquiry in Canada in the case I suggested, and where it may be proper to hold an inquiry. Take the case of a steamer which sinks another steamer and afterwards arrives in Great
Britain, She then leaves the United Kingdom and she comes to Canada. It might be possible to hold this inquiry in Canada as the witnesses are here, but this section would preclude that. The hon. gentleman will remember the case of the steamer La Bourgogne. She was sunk by another steamer, which came to Halifax. An inquiry was directed by the hon. gentleman. If we had to depend, as we might have had to depend upon the evidence of the sailors who were s.-tved from that ship, no inquiry could have been held in Canada, but as it turned out there were persons within Canada who belonged to the other colliding ship, which had not been sunk. That might happen in the United Kingdom. It seems to me that we should have an opportunity to hold the inquiry here.

I should like to agree with my hon. friend (Mr. Borden, Halifax), but I think he misconceives the force of the word ' seized.' It means that if the courts in England becomes possessed of the case they hold it. If they abandon it, any other jurisdiction can assume it. The first magistrate who is seized with the jurisdiction in a criminal case excludes all others, but in case he abandons it all other jurisdictions are open to deal with. It is the same in this ?

I think the hon. gentleman (Mr. Gourley) is right. The idea is to prevent two conflicting inquiries going on at the same time. What my hon. friend (Mr. Borden, Halifax) would suggest is: to add the words ' unless and until such investigation or inquiry in the United Kingdom has been abandoned or proved inoperative.'
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: That is the common law.
I do not think the section means that without some such words as the minister suggests.
The section might be allowed to pass as it is now and before the third reading we will consider it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Is it conceded that in the case of a vessel damaged in a canal it may properly be a case of inquiry ? That is rather important. In many cases, while the lock or the wall of the canal has been damaged the vessel herself has been very seriously damaged, and in one case that I know of, there was loss of life. These two points make it a casualty within the meaning of the Act: and in that case an inquiry should be made.
What is the question-whether a canal is a navigable water within the meaning of the Act ?
I understand that a canal is a navigable water. A vessel may be damaged in a canal, and in one case there was loss of life resulting from a collision.
I see no reason why the Act should not apply in such a case.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
I would be inclined to think that if a vessel took ground in a canal, this Act would apply. I think it would also apply if she struck the side of a canal, and were damaged in that way.

Bill (No. 66) further to amend the Canada Evidence Act, 1803 (the Solicitor General), read the second time, and House went into committee thereon.
On section 1,
Is the proviso in this section that the answer of a witness may not be used against him ?

The statute now makes provision that the answer of a witness shall not be available against him in inquiries over which this parliament has jurisdiction. The intention is to extend this proviso to inquiries under a statute of a province.

I should think it a very proper amendment.
